extraction.research_question: Do social connections (cosponsorship ties among members of Congress) causally raise legislative effectiveness, once the endogeneity of those ties is controlled, and does the network effect predicted by the model beat traditional centrality measures?
extraction.data: Legislative Effectiveness Scores (LES) for U.S. House members from Volden and Wiseman (2014), 109th to 113th Congresses (election cycles 2004 to 2012). Unit: member-congress; N = 2,176 connected congressmen (about 433 Representatives per Congress, including midterm replacements). Cosponsorship network built from THOMAS: two members linked if they cosponsored the same bill, weights = shared bills over total bills cosponsored. Instrument network: alumni ties from the Biographical Directory of Congress, two members linked if they attended the same institution within an 8-year window; about 40 percent of members linked. First-stage dyadic sample: 945,382 dyads (Table 1). Controls: seniority, margin of victory, DW-NOMINATE distance to median, size of state delegation, gender, race, party, committee chair, majority and minority leader, Speaker, Congress fixed effects.
extraction.method: Structural model yields equilibrium effectiveness E = [I - phi W]^-1 (beta x + epsilon) style spatial autoregressive system (eqs 5-7). Estimated by nonlinear least squares (NLLS). Endogeneity handled by a two-step Heckman-type control function: first stage dyadic OLS of cosponsorship links on alumni links, covariates and absolute differences; selection term xi built from first-stage residuals and inserted in the outcome equation (eqs 8-10). Standard errors from residual bootstrap with 500 replications resampling structural errors by Congress. Partial F tests for phi = 0. Robustness: committee fixed effects (21 committees), state legislative experience subsample, heterogeneous spillovers (eqs 11-14), within- versus between-party networks (eqs 15-17), outcome split by legislative stage (Table 7).
extraction.scope: U.S. House of Representatives only (the Senate is discussed but not analyzed), 109th to 113th Congresses (2004 to 2012 election cycles). The sample covers members with cosponsorship and alumni data, so 2,176 member-congress observations rather than all members. Results are for LES as defined by Volden and Wiseman.
key_findings: Theory (Sec 2.2, Proposition 1): unique Nash equilibrium in which effectiveness equals a weighted Katz-Bonacich centrality of the social network, given Assumption 1 (invertibility). With no spillovers the model reduces to the standard characteristics-only model.
Uncorrected NLLS (Table 2, col 2): network spillover phi = 0.4448 (SE 0.0233); partial F test of phi = 0 gives 350.81, reported p below 0.001. Positive and significant, consistent with externalities.

Corrected NLLS (Table 2, col 3, bootstrap SE): phi = 0.8324 (SE 0.0516); selection term xi = -0.4133 (SE 0.0741), significant; partial F = 59.51. Phi rises and stays significant after correction, which the authors read as network endogeneity biasing naive estimates downward for phi and biasing characteristic effects upward.

Committee chair effect (Table 2, Sec 4, p.16-17): OLS 1.9669 (SE 0.1147) versus 1.6107 (SE 0.1545) in the corrected network model, about 18 percent smaller in magnitude. The authors say OLS partly captures network effects.

Traditional centralities (Table 4): OLS betweenness 0.0079, closeness 0.0011 and eigenvector 0.1203 are all significant, but after the correction none is significant (betweenness -0.2599 SE 0.1662; closeness 0.0085 SE 0.0086; eigenvector -0.4122 SE 0.2500).

Horse race (Table 4, last block): when the model term is included with the other centralities, only phi stays significant; reported Phi = 0.7095 (SE 0.0817). Text cites this as Column (8) but the table header lists seven columns, so the column mapping is uncertain.

First stage (Table 1, 945,382 dyads): alumni-tie coefficient 3.8658 (SE 0.194) with full controls, stated as multiplied by hundreds; R-squared rises from 0.0007 (alumni only) to about 0.079 with controls, supporting alumni ties as a predictor of cosponsorship links.

Heterogeneous spillovers (Tables 5a and 5b, as parsed): the susceptibility coefficient for No White is 0.1584 (SE 0.0955, significant at 10 percent); seniority is -0.0339 (SE 0.0123); the committee-chair cell is -0.5981 (SE 0.1588). Text: minorities gain more, senior members and chairs gain less.

Party ties (Table 6): the between-party term is 0.8668 (SE 0.2136) and the within-party term 0.8346 (SE 0.0584) in the last column; the first column has 1.5984 (SE 0.4742) vs 1.4208 (SE 0.1000). The gap is small relative to SEs in the corrected columns, so the claim that cross-party ties matter more is only weakly supported in these numbers.

Legislative stage (Table 7, corrected Phi): BILL only 0.5634 (SE 0.0539); BILL plus AIC 0.8387 (SE 0.0465); ABC plus PASS plus LAW 0.8643 (SE 0.0767). Network effects are positive and significant at all stages and larger later; xi is significant in each corrected column.

Robustness (Table 8): with committee fixed effects, corrected Phi = 0.7114 (SE 0.0664) on N = 2,176; on the state-experience subsample (N = 1,775) corrected Phi = 0.8150 (SE 0.0517). Estimates are stable; table column labels conflict with the text on which columns carry committee dummies.
limitations: Working paper, not peer-reviewed (NBER disclaimer, p.1).

Identification relies on the alumni network being exogenous to politics and relevant for cosponsorship; the paper asserts this and gives no formal exclusion test. Footnote 5 notes identification may also come from nonlinearities alone.
Selection term xi is a generated regressor; bootstrap resamples structural errors only, and the authors note no closed-form NLLS standard errors exist in this network setting.
Alumni links cover only about 40 percent of members, so the sample is 2,176 member-congress observations, not the full chamber.
Assumption 1 (invertibility, positivity) is assumed for the empirical range, not verified; the authors say it fails only with very large spillovers.
Model and results are for House LES only; the Senate is not analyzed and LES is a single composite index with weights set by Volden and Wiseman.
Text calls the correction Heckman but the procedure is a two-step control function, as the paper's own footnote 4 notes (citing Qu and Lee 2015).
Table and text references conflict: horse-race column (8) vs seven headed columns; committee dummies placed in Table 8 columns 5-6 in the table but in columns 1-2 in the text.

extraction.theory: Each legislator chooses effort to maximize his own effectiveness, which depends on his characteristics, his effort, and the effectiveness of socially connected colleagues weighted by tie strength (complementarity between own effort and peers' effectiveness). Simultaneous effort choice gives a linear equilibrium in which effectiveness is a weighted Katz-Bonacich centrality (Ballester, Calvo-Armengol and Zenou 2006 style) with weights set by member characteristics. The paper says the equilibrium is unique under Assumption 1 and that the model nests the standard characteristics-only regression at phi = 0.
extraction.identification: Two-step control function (Heckman-type) for an endogenous network. Stage 1: dyadic link-formation regression of cosponsorship ties on alumni ties, dyad-level differences in characteristics (absolute values), and covariates. Stage 2: NLLS of the spatial model with xi, the function of stage-1 residuals, added to the outcome equation; joint normality (Assumption 2) implies a common selection effect across members. Exclusion restriction: alumni ties affect LES only through cosponsorship. Footnote 5 says identification could come from nonlinearity without exclusion restrictions.
extraction.measures: Outcome: Legislative Effectiveness Score (LES), weighted average of BILL, AIC, ABC, PASS and LAW indicators normalized to mean 1 per Congress (mean 1.0081, SD 1.47 in Table A.1). Network: cosponsorship share and alumni share (institutions shared within 8 years over institutions attended). Centralities: Bonacich (model), betweenness, closeness, eigenvector. Controls: seniority, margin of victory (vote share), DW-NOMINATE absolute first dimension (distance to median), delegation size, party, gender, race (No White), committee chair, majority and minority leader, Speaker.

summary_md: Battaglini, Leone Sciabolazza and Patacchini (NBER WP 24442, 2018; a working paper, not peer reviewed) model House members who put effort into lawmaking and gain from the effectiveness of the colleagues they cosponsor with. In equilibrium, a member's Volden-Wiseman Legislative Effectiveness Score (LES) is proportional to a characteristic-weighted Katz-Bonacich centrality of the cosponsorship network. They estimate this by nonlinear least squares on 2,176 member-Congress observations (House, 109th to 113th Congresses). Cosponsorship ties are endogenous, so they correct with a two-step control function that uses shared-alma-mater ties as the instrument (first stage on 945,382 dyads). The spillover parameter phi is 0.44 uncorrected and 0.83 corrected (SE 0.05). The selection term is significant. Betweenness, closeness and eigenvector centrality are each significant in naive OLS, but none is significant after the correction. In a horse race, only the model-derived Katz-Bonacich term survives (phi 0.71). The committee-chair effect shrinks about 18 percent (1.97 to 1.61) once the network enters the model. Network effects are positive at every stage from BILL to LAW and grow at later stages. Cross-party and within-party ties have similar coefficients (0.87 vs 0.83), and the gap is small next to their standard errors. For Paul's systems, the paper is the empirical twin of the 2016 targeting paper behind the diagnostic Katz-Bonacich benchmark. It supports the June decision to retire the direction-blind InfluenceScore blend. It also flags that the live cosponsor graph is used without any endogeneity correction. The system already loads CEL LES data, so a direct replication of this paper's KB-to-LES link is cheap. That replication has not been run, and any such result stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it.

summary_issues: Prop 1 states that effectiveness equals the characteristic-weighted Bonacich centrality, not that it is proportional to it. The summary and bearing 1 should say equal to.

The summary says the paper supports retiring the direction-blind InfluenceScore. The paper does not discuss edge direction; it only shows the centralities drop out after the tie correction. Recast as independent corroboration of a null.

Table 6 is not the only stratification. Tables 5a and 5b (No White, seniority, chair susceptibility), the Table 7 stage split, the Table 8 state-experience subsample (N = 1,775) and committee fixed effects are also reported. Phi 0.83 is pooled over House members, 109th-113th.
The Table 4 note says betweenness, closeness and eigenvector coefficients are on centralities multiplied by 100, 10,000 and 10,000. The summary quotes them unscaled and should carry the scale.
The summary omits that the authors' text says cross-party ties matter more (Sec 5.2 and Conclusion), while Table 6 shows near-equal coefficients. Report both.
Text and table disagree on the horse-race column (text cites col 8; the table has 7 columns) and on which Table 8 columns carry committee dummies. Cite table numbers, not text column labels.
The alumni figure 0.0387 per dyad is Table 1 col 2 only. Col 3 with full controls gives 0.0386. The ext label full controls for 3.8658 is loose.
Gap 2 says both the 2016 and 2018 papers use characteristic-weighted KB on a row-share matrix. Only the 2018 paper was checked here; the 2016 text was not read.
Paul alignment (Ardekani and Sotoudeh highlights, unannotated 2016 entry) could not be verified from the item files. Treat it as unverified.

The row-share recomputation (bearing 1) and the first test (bearing 4) point toward the per-member normalization class this project rejected. Keep them as flagged UNVERIFIED tests, not recommendations.
The claim that CEL LES has never been regressed on KB was checked only as far as lep_criterion.py; it is not confirmed for the whole repo.

Two code citations were wrong: InfluenceScore weights point to the June network plan line 25, and the chair multiplier points to the rules-scoring file line 37 (workbook line 117 is a table header). Fixed in bearings 2 and 7.
Working-paper status is confirmed by the NBER disclaimer (not peer reviewed). The horse-race and Table 8 column conflicts flagged by the rel are confirmed.
gaps_exposed: kb_benchmark.py labels MBC.scores() as the legislative score, but moneyball_core.py:252 returns the composite four-pillar score. The 2026-08-18 rho of +0.65 (n = 533) is KB versus the composite, not versus the legislative pillar or LES.

kb_benchmark.py uses an unweighted unit vector on the saturated build_P kernel. Neither the 2016 nor the 2018 papers use that form: both use characteristic-weighted KB on a row-share cosponsor matrix. The benchmark is a loose analogue, not a replication.

The CEL LES data are already loaded (fec/members/lep_criterion.py) but have never been regressed on KB or network spillovers. That makes the paper's central result a cheap read-only replication target, which has not been attempted.
No component treats cosponsorship ties as endogenous. All centralities, the cascade kernel and recruitment routes take the observed graph as exogenous, and nothing addresses selection into ties.
The undervaluation lens still uses Centrality% from the retired InfluenceScore blend. The paper finds no predictive value for those centralities once tie selection is corrected.
The effectiveness shadow has no peer-spillover term, although the paper finds spillovers at every one of its five stages.
flags: The paper's edge weight is shared bills over the member's total cosponsored bills, a per-member volume normalization. This project measured and rejected per-edge volume normalization, so do not adopt the paper's weighting into the live graph.

Alumni (shared-background) ties appear here only as an instrument for link formation. Under D-025, any shared-background score in Paul's systems remains a heuristic, never a closeness or introduction probability.

The paper's phi (0.83) is pooled across five Congresses and both parties. Its only stratification is the within- versus between-party tie split in Table 6. Quote phi as pooled, House only, 109th-113th.
Working paper, not peer reviewed. The text and tables disagree on the horse-race column and on which Table 8 columns carry committee dummies.
Any replication of KB to LES on Paul's graph is new agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
paul_alignment: Paul has no annotation for this work. Under the Katz-Bonacich benchmark he lists only the 2016 companion paper, unannotated. He highlighted Ardekani's preference for Katz centrality and Sotoudeh's weak result for eigenvector centrality. This paper agrees with both: only the model-derived Katz-Bonacich term survives the correction. His position is not stale, but the benchmark is mislabeled (it scores against the composite) and has never been tested against the CEL LES data already on hand.

Table 1 (4-8), training (8), zero-shot results (9-11), few-shot results (12-14), timing (14-15), limitations and model use (15-17), conclusion (17-18), references, Appendices A-C (19-26). Metadata hints checked: title, four authors, year 2024 and preprint status are correct; venue arXiv; no DOI in text. Topic check: the paper has no lobbying, network, path-finding, allocation, election, persuasion or turnout content. Legislators appear only as stance targets in the PolNLI sources (Polistance datasets, p.23). Text measurement is the whole paper. Reader observation, not an authors claim: GPT-4o relabeling and filtering (p.6-7) and GPT-4o hypothesis augmentation (p.7) mean the PolNLI labels share an LLM source; the authors exclude GPT-4o from the benchmark for that reason (p.10). Figure values (Figs 1-5) are not in the text, so per-model MCC and timing figures are not extracted.
extraction.research_question: Can small, domain-adapted natural language inference (NLI) encoder models trained on political text match or beat zero-shot large language models and supervised classifiers for political text classification, and can they be few-shot trained from 10-25 labeled documents, while staying open and efficient? (p.1-2)
extraction.theory: No formal theory. Argument: NLI framing turns any classification into a document-hypothesis entailment task, and narrowing a small pretrained encoder to one domain reduces the model size needed for high performance; transfer from general NLI models speeds adaptation (p.2-4, p.8).
extraction.data: PolNLI: 201,691 political documents, 852 unique entailment hypotheses, 22 datasets in four tasks: stance 11 datasets, 361 hypotheses, 66,581 documents; topic 5, 278, 62,005; hate-speech/toxicity 2, 177, 41,871; event extraction 4, 36, 31,234 (Table 1, p.5). Sources include tweets, news, congressional newsletters, legislation, party platforms, State of the Union speeches, Supreme Court case summaries, ACLED and SCAD event records, and crowd-sourced arguments (Appendix A, p.23). Unit: document paired with a hypothesis, labeled entail or not entail. After augmentation there are 2,834 unique entailment phrasings (p.7). Split: test and validation sets of about 15,000 documents each, split by hypothesis so test hypotheses are unseen in training; validation is about 10,000 unseen-hypothesis and 5,000 seen-hypothesis documents (p.7-8). Few-shot test cases: Mood of the Nation open-text democracy answers (liberty and rights) and COVID-19 threat-minimization tweets, about 2,000 tweets in Block Jr. et al. (p.12-14). Timing: 5,000 PolNLI test documents (p.14).
extraction.method: Fine-tunes DeBERTa V3 base (86M parameters) and large (304M) models that were already trained for general NLI (Laurer et al. 2023), using the Transformers library (p.2, p.8). Label cleaning removes source metadata; hypotheses are written per label (p.5-6). Labels are validated by GPT-4o; documents where human and LLM labels disagree are dropped (p.6-7). Hypotheses are augmented with GPT-4o synonyms and manual review (p.7). Checkpoints chosen by training loss, validation loss, MCC, F1, accuracy and per-task consistency, plus qualitative tests with punctuation, capitalization and wording edits (p.8). Zero-shot benchmark against DeBERTa base and large NLI (Laurer et al. 2023), Llama 3.1 8B and Claude 3.5 Sonnet; GPT-4o not benchmarked (p.9). Few-shot: simple random samples of 10, 25, 50 and 100 documents, 10 repetitions each, 95% confidence intervals, default learning rate, 5 epochs, no hyperparameter or hypothesis search (p.12). Timing: same 5,000 documents with hypothesis 'This text is about politics' on RTX 3090, Tesla T4, M3 Max and Ryzen 9 5900x (p.14).
extraction.identification: Not causal. Generalization is judged by splitting test documents on unseen hypotheses (p.7-8) and by few-shot learning curves at sample sizes 10, 25, 50 and 100 (p.12).
extraction.measures: Primary metric: Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), chosen for robustness on binary tasks (p.9). Also accuracy and F1 (checkpoint selection, p.8; COVID accuracy, p.14; Llama accuracy, p.13). Bootstrapped standard errors for Fig. 1 (p.9-10); 95% confidence intervals across 10 few-shot repetitions (p.12). Timing: documents per second by hardware (Fig. 5, p.15; values not in text).
extraction.scope: Population: English-language political text from social media, news, newsletters, legislation, party platforms, speeches, court summaries, event reports and crowd-sourced arguments (Appendix A, p.23). Language: English only (p.17). Era: sources span several years; references were accessed in June 2024 (p.19-22). Tasks: stance, topic, hate-speech and toxicity, and event classification (p.4).
key_findings: PolNLI test set, all tasks combined: DEBATE models are more performative than DeBERTa base and large NLI, Llama 3.1 8B and Claude 3.5 Sonnet in zero-shot MCC; per-model values appear only in Fig. 1 (p.9-10).
Stance: DEBATE models and Claude 3.5 Sonnet are significantly better than the other models on stance detection; event extraction is comparable between DEBATE and the two LLMs (p.9).
Hate-speech: DEBATE models are significantly better than the other models; the authors attribute this to subjective definitions that the models were tuned to (p.9-10).
Polistance Quote Tweets (stance, hardest set): Claude 3.5 MCC 0.29; DEBATE base MCC 0.62 and large MCC 0.88; DeBERTa Large had negative correlation with the correct label on this dataset (p.10).

Few-shot, Mood of the Nation liberty and rights: Llama 3.1 is best zero-shot (reported MCC 0.74, accuracy 88%); after 10 samples both DEBATE models jump and do not differ significantly from Llama; at 25 the large model significantly beats Llama; at 50 the base model matches it (p.13).

Few-shot, COVID-19 threat minimization: base model largely fails zero-shot and does not match the supervised Electra classifier (MCC 0.66 on 2,000 tweets) at 100 samples; large model matches it at 10 samples (MCC 0.67, accuracy 87%) and exceeds it at 25 (MCC 0.69, accuracy 88%) (p.13-14).

Efficiency: DEBATE models give large speed advantages over Llama 3.1 8B on all four tested hardware types; a laptop GPU (M3 Max) or free cloud GPU (Tesla T4) classifies documents at a brisk pace; exact timings are in Fig. 5 only (p.14-15).
Training: base model learning rate 2e-5, batch 8, 20 epochs; large model learning rate 9e-6, batch 4 with gradient accumulation 4, 20 epochs; checkpoint per epoch (Appendix C, p.25-26).
Recommendation: use the large model for zero-shot and most few-shot work; the base model for simple few-shot or supervised work (p.15-16).
Recommendation: keep NLI hypotheses short and template-like; use few-shot training when a task needs long hypotheses with several conditions, or is far from the PolNLI sources (p.16-17).
Stated limitation with a finding: the authors do not expect DEBATE to beat proprietary LLMs on all tasks; LLMs are expected to generalize better to tasks far from PolNLI (p.17).
Validation: GPT-4o labels matched manual review on 92.5% of 400 sampled documents (Cohen's kappa 0.85); 14 of 400 (3.5%) were judged wrong LLM labels (p.7).
limitations: Trained and evaluated only on English documents; performance on other languages is unknown (p.17).
Not expected to outperform proprietary LLMs on every task; LLMs expected to generalize better to tasks far from PolNLI (p.17).
NLI hypotheses must be short; no clear measure of task simplicity exists, only qualitative judgments (p.16).
Labels for topic and event data were positive-only; negatives were created by random reassignment, and multi-topic documents are a known concern addressed only by validation (p.6-7).
Authors discourage benchmarking OpenAI models on PolNLI because GPT-4o was used in label validation (p.10).
Few-shot runs used no hyperparameter or hypothesis search, by design, so the results are not tuned (p.12).
short_quotes: A simple random sample of only 10-25 labeled documents is sufficient to teach the models complex labeling tasks when necessary.
Because of this, it is little wonder that LLMs have received widespread adoption within political and other social sciences.

summary_md: Burnham, Kahn, Wang and Peng (arXiv 2024) release Political DEBATE: DeBERTa V3 base (86M) and large (304M) NLI classifiers, further trained on PolNLI. PolNLI holds 201,691 political documents and 852 hypotheses across stance, topic, hate-speech and event tasks, and its sources include congressional newsletters. On test hypotheses unseen in training, both models beat general NLI models, Llama 3.1 8B and Claude 3.5 Sonnet on zero-shot MCC. On the hardest stance set (quote tweets), Claude scores MCC 0.29, base 0.62 and large 0.88. In few-shot training, 10 to 25 random labeled documents are often enough. The base model, however, failed the bespoke COVID threat-minimization task and could not match a supervised classifier (MCC 0.66) even at 100 samples, while the large model matched it at 10 (0.67). The authors therefore recommend the large model whenever feasible, short single-condition hypotheses, and supervised training when labels need meta-knowledge or a bespoke concept. The labels were validated with GPT-4o, so GPT-4o is excluded from the benchmark. For Paul, this is the actual checkpoint behind the Melange CU press stance reader. The system fine-tunes the base model on 552 labeled releases. Its own history follows the paper's pattern: base zero-shot reached 53% accuracy with oppose F1 0.08, and fine-tuning raised it to 87% agreement with Claude. Its valence-hop bottleneck matches the paper's warning about bespoke concepts. The bearings are on the model choice (base, not large), hypothesis design (a compound neutral hypothesis), the evaluation metric (accuracy and kappa against an LLM reference rather than MCC against humans), and the planned ACU speaker-mode branching. Nothing here touches the SNA or LDA rules.

extraction.research_question: How should difference-in-differences designs with a continuous or multi-valued dose be identified, interpreted and estimated? Which causal parameters are identified under standard parallel trends versus stronger assumptions, and what does the common two-way fixed effects (TWFE) regression with a dose-by-post interaction actually estimate?
extraction.theory: Potential outcomes indexed by dose (Robins 1986). Distinguishes level treatment effects Y(d)-Y(0) from causal responses, the marginal derivative in dose (Angrist and Imbens 1995). Generalizes Fricke (2017) from two doses to continuous and multi-valued doses. Uses Yitzhaki (1996) linear-projection decomposition of regression slopes. The empirical interpretation of the derivative as an elasticity of substitution comes from a homothetic two-factor hospital production model following Acemoglu and Finkelstein (2008).
extraction.data: Application: Acemoglu and Finkelstein (2008) AHA Annual Survey Database hospital panel. Balanced panel of 5881 hospitals; pre period averaged over 1980-1983 and post period over 1984-1986 (Sec 6, p.25). Dose M is the 1983 Medicare inpatient share; among treated hospitals mean 0.45, SD 0.15 (Sec 2, p.5). 4987 hospitals have a positive dose; 57 above 0.75, 20 above 0.80, 3 above 0.90 (Sec 6.2, p.28). Outcome is the depreciation share of total operating expenses as a capital-labor proxy; 1983 mean 4.5; untreated mean change 0.37 (Fig 4 note, p.27). Figure 1 uses 1980-1986 annual data and drops 860 of 6741 hospitals with missing outcomes. Policy: 1983 PPS set the labor subsidy to zero and left the capital subsidy unchanged.
extraction.method: Two-period DiD with continuous dose, identified under parallel trends (PT, Assumption PT) and strong parallel trends (SPT, Assumption SPT). Estimators: (i) binarized DiD regression of the outcome change on an indicator for positive dose (eq 4.6), which recovers ATT_glob under SPT; (ii) saturated regression with dose dummies for discrete doses (eq 4.1); (iii) quadratic parametric regression among treated units (eq 4.2); (iv) nonparametric sieve regression with cubic B-splines and a data-driven Lepski-type sieve dimension (Chen, Christensen and Kankanala 2025), with honest uniform confidence bands (Appendix B). ACRT_glob is the sample mean of estimated ACRT(D_i) over treated units. TWFE is decomposed (Theorem 3.4) into causal response, levels, scaled levels and scaled 2x2 representations with explicit weights (Table 1). Extensions: staggered timing (Appendix C), relaxing SPT through bounds, sub-regions and covariate-conditional SPT (Sec 5). Pre-trend checks use event-study versions ATT_loc(e) and ACRT_loc(e). Inference clusters at the hospital level.
extraction.identification: Under PT, ATT(d|d) = E[dY|D=d] - E[dY|D=0] and ATT_loc = E[dY|D>0] - E[dY|D=0] are identified, but comparisons across dose groups mix causal responses with selection bias (Thm 3.1, 3.2). Under SPT, ATT(d) and ACRT(d) are identified, and ATT_glob = E[dY|D>0] - E[dY|D=0] and ACRT_glob = E of the dose-density-weighted derivative of E[dY|D=d] (Thm 3.3, Cor 3.1). Without untreated units, the dose-group comparison to the lowest dose recovers differences only, and interpreting them causally requires strengthening PT (Remark 3.1). Pre-period data cannot test SPT (p.13-14).

extraction.scope: Population: US hospitals in the Acemoglu and Finkelstein balanced panel subject to the 1983 Medicare PPS labor-subsidy change. Era: 1980-1986. The identification and estimation results apply to any two-period DiD with a continuous or multi-valued dose, and to staggered designs in Appendix C. The empirical content is a single application, not a general estimate.
key_findings: Under PT, ATT(d|d) and ATT_loc = E[dY|D>0] - E[dY|D=0] are identified (Thm 3.1, p.10). The main text makes clear that ATT(d) is not identified under PT alone.
Under PT alone, comparing outcome paths across dose groups mixes a causal response with a selection bias term ATT(l|h) - ATT(l|l); causal responses are not identified (Thm 3.2, p.11).
Under SPT, ATT(d), ACRT(d), ATT_glob and ACRT_glob are identified; ACRT_glob equals the average derivative weighted by the dose density among treated (Thm 3.3, Cor 3.1, p.12-14).
The TWFE coefficient is a weighted integral of ATT(d|d) whose weights integrate to zero, with negative weights below the mean dose and positive above (Thm 3.4(b), p.16-17).

Under PT, the TWFE causal-response decomposition is a convex average of ACRT(d|d) plus selection bias, with positive weights integrating to one (Thm 3.4(a), p.16). Positive weights do not make TWFE a natural target.
Equation 3.1 writes beta_twfe as a Wald-type ratio with distance weights; in the application the numerator is 0.60 and the denominator 0.53 (p.17, p.28).
Nonparametric ATT_loc = 0.80 (s.e. 0.05), about 18 percent of the 1983 mean outcome of 4.5; reject zero for doses 0.05 to 0.78, covering 96 percent of treated hospitals (Sec 6.2, p.27).

Static TWFE coefficient is 1.14 (s.e. 0.099, Fig 1); it is close to ATT_loc only because two biases offset. Dropping untreated units shrinks TWFE by 78 percent while causal responses are unchanged (p.3, p.28, p.30).
ACRT_glob = -0.08 (s.e. 0.19), not significantly different from zero; estimated ACRT(m) is negative for m above 0.41, covering 71 percent of treated hospitals (Sec 6.3, p.30).
Post-period average of the ATT event study is 0.755 (s.e. 0.048) (Fig 8, p.30); post-period average of the ACRT event study is 0.220 (s.e. 0.170) (Fig 10, p.32).
Pre-treatment ACRT event-study estimates reject the zero implied by no-anticipation plus parallel trends in 1981, though the violation is small relative to post-period effects (p.32).

Implied average elasticity of substitution point estimates do not fit the positive-elasticity prediction, although the uniform bands do not reject zero; the authors treat this as evidence against SPT or the two-factor model (p.31-32).
limitations: SPT is described as strong and perhaps implausible in many applications; the authors do not propose it as a default (p.13).
Pre-trend tests cannot distinguish PT from SPT, because pre-period outcomes are untreated potential outcomes (p.13-14).

Event-study pre-trend tests may miss PT violations; aggregate PT allows violations that average to zero across dose groups, and whether that should count as evidence against the design is debated (p.24-25).

Quadratic parametric estimates are precise only if the functional form is correct; pretesting parametric against nonparametric fits can mislead, so the authors use honest nonparametric bands (p.28-29).
Nonparametric precision is limited where doses are sparse, with only 57 treated hospitals above dose 0.75 (p.28).
Footnote 12: the sieve dimension used for ACRT_glob is treated as non-random; the randomness of the Lepski-type selection is left for future research (p.30).
A Neyman-orthogonal representation for ACRT_glob suggests double machine learning, which the paper leaves for future research (p.22).
Without untreated units, ATT(d|d) and the levels decompositions are not identified; only dose-group differences are identified (Remark 3.1, Remark 3.2, p.14-15).
The 1983 pre-PPS event-study coefficient may reflect partial 1983 PPS effects and fiscal-year reporting (footnote 11, p.29).

The elasticity interpretation assumes no anticipation and a homothetic two-factor production model; the authors note alternatives such as a three-factor or non-homothetic model could rationalize the negative ACRT (p.31-32).

Formal estimation for the staggered case is not provided; the authors say disaggregated results apply directly and that binarized event-study procedures can be used when ATT_loc(e) is the target (Remark C.1, p.42).
TWFE beta depends on the unit of dose: recoding the dose from 0 to 100 shrinks beta from 1.14 to 0.0114 while ATT_loc is unchanged (p.28).

summary_md: Callaway, Goodman-Bacon and Sant'Anna (arXiv 2107.02637v8, 2025) work out what difference-in-differences identifies when treatment comes as a continuous dose rather than an on/off switch. Under ordinary parallel trends, only effects for the units that actually got dose d are identified (ATT(d|d), and ATT_loc pooled over treated units). Comparing outcomes across dose levels mixes the causal response with a selection-bias term (Thm 3.2). Causal responses such as ACRT(d), the derivative in dose, need strong parallel trends: the response to each dose must be the same across dose groups. Pre-period data cannot test that assumption. The common two-way fixed effects (TWFE) dose-by-post slope is a weighted average with non-obvious weights. In the levels form those weights integrate to zero and are negative below the mean dose (Thm 3.4). The slope also depends on the dose units and on whether untreated units are included. In the Medicare PPS hospital application (5,881 hospitals, 1980-1986), TWFE gives 1.14. That sits near ATT_loc = 0.80 only because two biases offset. ACRT_glob = -0.08 (s.e. 0.19), and dropping untreated units shrinks TWFE by 78 percent while the causal responses do not move. Estimation uses binarized DiD plus B-spline sieve regressions with honest uniform bands. The paper bears most on the Mentat sector-growth regressions, which put a continuous growth measure into sector-plus-year fixed-effects models with no zero-dose group. It also bears, as a design template, on the open question of whether money's effect is concave, which the Melange money terms assume but never estimate. Purely econometric. No lobbying, network or legislator content.

Text-measurement, persuasion-adjacent and election-adjacent passages read in full; lobbying, networks, path-finding, allocation and turnout are absent from the paper (only cited as background, e.g. politicians' perceived personality and electoral success, CEO perception and firm value). No page images rendered. Paul annotations: none; item lists no annot_sha12s and no _annots file exists for sha 31ea20118bb8, so paul_markup is empty. ext and rel sidecars: not present. Metadata hints corrected: doi was blank and is 10.1038/s41598-024-57271-z per the text header; title, authors, year and venue confirmed.
extraction.research_question: Can the perceived personality of public figures (Big Five traits and likability) be predicted from the location of their names in GPT-3's semantic embedding space, and does this hold after controlling for likability and demographics?
extraction.theory: Perceptions of others' personality are consequential and matter regardless of accuracy. Word embeddings act as a functional analogue of human semantic memory and encode word meanings, group stereotypes, and (per the authors) individual differences. The authors also invoke the personality halo effect, where likable people are perceived as having desirable personalities, as the reason likability and demographics explain part of the signal.
extraction.data: Sample of 226 public figures (N = 226) drawn from the 300 most popular figures among 11,341 in the Pantheon 1.0 dataset, across 43 countries; born 1900 or later; artists capped at 100; popularity proxied by Wikipedia page views 2008-2013; 74 figures removed for fewer than 10 raters. Human ratings from 600 Prolific raters, each rating 10 random figures on likability (200-point scale) and Big Five traits via the 10-item TIPI; mean 18.89 ratings per figure (SD 10.38). Predictors are 12,288-dimensional GPT-3 embeddings of each name. Unit of analysis: public figure. Data and code on OSF (854w2).
extraction.method: Ridge regression of mean human ratings on column-standardized GPT-3 name embeddings, with 20-fold cross-validation (each figure predicted by a model trained on all others) and alpha tuned in an inner 20-fold loop. Controlled models first regress each trait on likability plus demographics (birth year, gender) and then predict the residuals from embeddings. Correlations are corrected for attenuation by dividing by the square root of split-half reliability (0.79-0.88). Effect sizes converted to Cohen's d. Interpretation by projecting 525 person-descriptive adjectives onto the fitted regression lines.
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. The design is out-of-sample predictive validity (cross-validation) with face-validity checks (top and bottom figures, adjective extremes). No causal claim is made about embeddings producing perceptions.
extraction.measures: Outcomes: mean human ratings per public figure of likability (200-point scale) and TIPI-based Big Five (openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, emotional stability). Reliability: split-half reliability 0.79-0.88 used as ceiling; ICC reported in supplement. Predictors: GPT-3 name embeddings (12,288 dims). Controls: likability, birth year, gender. Popularity: log Wikipedia page views (r = 0.16 with profile similarity).
extraction.scope: Population: globally famous public figures in Pantheon 1.0 with sufficient rater coverage, born 1900 or later, from 43 countries. Era: the GPT-3 training corpus, whose date range the text does not state; the authors note predictions reflect only the training-data period. Not tested on private individuals or on people absent from the training data.
key_findings: Without controls, cross-validated predictions correlate with human ratings r = 0.78 (extraversion) to 0.88 (openness) after attenuation correction; raw r 0.70-0.80. Results p.2 and Figure 1 green bars.
Translated to Cohen's d, the no-controls correlations give d = 2.49 to 3.75 (labelled huge effects). Results p.2.

Controlling for likability and demographics, accuracy falls to r = 0.53 (emotional stability) to 0.70 (extraversion) after correction; raw r 0.43-0.61 (d = 1.25-1.96). Results p.4 and Figure 1 red bars.

Benchmarks used by authors: no-controls accuracy compared with CT detection of head and neck metastases (r = 0.64) and ultrasound for peripheral artery disease (r = 0.83); controlled accuracy compared with dental X-ray cavity detection (r = 0.43) and ultrasound for deep venous thrombosis (r = 0.60). Results p.3-4.
Self-reported Big Five from language is cited as about r = 0.40 for comparison. Results p.4.
Embeddings predict aggregate human judgments better than individual judgments do: single-rater to aggregate correlation r = 0.56-0.66. Results p.3.
Accuracy is higher for more popular figures: profile similarity correlates with log Wikipedia page views at r = 0.16. Results p.3.

Face validity: top openness figures are mostly artists (Freddie Mercury, David Bowie, Michael Jackson, Lady Gaga, Jimi Hendrix, Quentin Tarantino); bottom openness includes Kim Jong-un, Kim Jong-il and conservative politicians. Results p.3-4, Table 1.

Adjective check across 525 person-descriptive adjectives: 'quiet', 'lonely', 'depressed' sit at the low extraversion pole and 'entertaining', 'hilarious', 'lively' at the high pole; 'alcoholic' ranks 3rd (of 525) for low conscientiousness and 3rd for low emotional stability. Results p.5, Table 3.

Birth year correlates with perceived extraversion: human ratings r = 0.35 and GPT-3 predictions r = 0.44 (text, p.4; Table 2). Women are perceived as more agreeable and are absent from the bottom of predicted agreeableness. Results p.4.
Perceived personality tracks likability: many of the least likable figures (Lee Harvey Oswald, Charles Manson, both Kims) sit at undesirable extremes of several traits. Results p.4.

Discussion argues that intimate traits of public figures can be extracted from widely available LLMs, framed as a privacy threat, and that the approach could extend to people absent from training data. Discussion p.6-7; the extension is not tested in the paper.
extraction.limitations: Requires collecting human ratings to train the regression (authors suggest adjective-distance or LLM-description approaches as untested substitutes). Predictions reflect only the period in the training data, so changed public perceptions lag until retraining. Extension to people absent from the training data is untested. Sample is 226 public figures after dropping 74 with fewer than 10 raters and excluding those born before 1900; raters were Prolific workers recognising the names. Correlations concern perceived, not actual, personality. Demographic and likability controls are partial. Authors note Wikipedia-based popularity is a proxy. Supplementary materials hold the ICC and popularity details, not read here.
short_quotes: We show that people's perceptions of public figures' personalities can be accurately predicted from their names' location in GPT-3's semantic space.
Even when controlling for demographics and likability, name embeddings allow for diagnosing public figures' perceived personalities.
Our models remained accurate even when controlling for public figures' demographics and overall likability.

summary_md: Cao and Kosinski (Scientific Reports 14:6735, 2024) fit ridge regressions from 12,288-dimensional GPT-3 embeddings of public figures' NAMES to mean human ratings of perceived Big Five traits and likability (N = 226 Pantheon figures from 43 countries, 600 Prolific raters, about 19 ratings per figure, TIPI items). With 20-fold cross-validation, predictions correlate with aggregate perceptions at r = .78 to .88 after attenuation correction (raw .70 to .80). Controlling for likability and demographics (birth year, gender), accuracy falls to corrected r = .53 to .70 (raw .43 to .61). Accuracy rises with popularity (r = .16 with log Wikipedia views). The design is predictive, not causal, and concerns PERCEIVED, not actual, personality. For Melange the paper is the cited motivation for de-identifying text before the Pink LLM trait reader: a model that knows a politician's name carries a reputational prior that can stand in for reading the text. The paper shows the prior exists for famous names; it does not test whether stripping names, titles, party and states from congressional text removes it, and the repo's --named contamination probe has no output artifact in data/members. The likability result bears on the halo questions: a large evaluative factor runs through perceptions of public figures, yet trait-specific signal survives its removal, consistent with the CT-CM design of one halo method factor plus traits, and a caution that perception-based gold panels are not halo-free criteria. The code cites the work as PNAS Nexus 2024 with r = .76 to .87; the vault copy is Scientific Reports with corrected r = .78 to .88, so that citation needs checking.

meta.title: Impressive Words: Linguistic Predictors of Public Approval of the U.S. Congress

extraction.title: Impressive Words: Linguistic Predictors of Public Approval of the U.S. Congress
extraction.document_type: empirical journal article (open access, Personality and Social Psychology section)
extraction.coverage: Read full text (64,859 chars, journal pp.1-13) in four chunks: front matter, abstract, intro, methods, Tables 1-6, results, discussion, conclusion, references. Nothing skipped. No annotation files exist (annot_sha12s empty), so paul_markup is empty and none dropped. Page images not rendered. Metadata: title, authors, year, venue correct; doi was blank, filled from text. Supplement not in text file, so its numbers are not extracted.
extraction.research_question: Which demeanor makes the best impression in a professional setting: agentic (competent) language, communal (warm) language, or a specific linguistic category? Tested by predicting monthly public approval of the U.S. Congress from the words used in House floor debates, first theory-driven, then exploratory.
extraction.theory: Agency and communion as the two primary dimensions of social cognition (Bakan 1966; Fiske et al 2002; Cuddy et al 2008). Communion is split into belonging (group intimacy) and prosociality (helping others), following Frimer et al 2011. H1: agentic and communal language both positively predict approval. H2: the prosocial facet, not communion broadly, predicts approval. H3a: communal language is a stronger predictor than agentic. H3b: agentic is stronger than communal. Exploratory: all 63 LIWC categories, to find blind spots in agency/communion theory.
extraction.data: House floor-debate transcripts, Jan 1996 to Nov 2014 (Congressional Record via GPO API; extension of remarks excluded); 123,781,226 words. 22 transcripts under 5,000 words dropped; 206 monthly transcripts analysed (N = 206 months). Outcome: monthly mean of Gallup approval polls (198 of 227 months polled; gaps interpolated; mean 33%, SD 15%). Controls: President news conferences (411; 2,205,168 words); BLS unemployment; Michigan consumer sentiment; partisan vote share (mean 43%); bills passed; vetoes; female and Democratic member shares; media tone (Frimer et al 2015).
extraction.method: Word density per LIWC 2007 category (63) plus a 127-word prosocial dictionary. Five blind coders scored each category +1, 0 or -1 for agency and communion (ICC communion 0.90, agency 0.82). Indexes = z-scored densities times weights, summed. Pearson correlations; OLS Models 1 to 3 (Model 3 adds controls); z tests comparing correlations; Hayes bootstrapped mediation via media tone; exploratory stepwise regression over 63 categories (entry p < 0.005, removal p > 0.01).
extraction.identification: None. The authors state the design is correlational and cannot show that congressional language influences approval; reverse causation and third variables are acknowledged. The only strategy is adding exogenous and endogenous covariates to Model 3 (and a 6-month lag found in Frimer et al 2015, cited but not modelled here). The mediation test checks indirect paths via media tone, not causal identification.
extraction.scope: Only the U.S. House of Representatives floor speech (not the Senate, committees or extension of remarks); public approval of Congress as a whole (not individual members); monthly aggregates over 1996 to 2014.
extraction.measures: Approval: monthly average of Gallup approve or disapprove items (dichotomous). Language: LIWC 2007 densities; agency and communion indexes from coder weights; prosocial dictionary density. Media: quantity times valence of editorials (Factiva; 9-point tone). Presidential rhetoric: the same dictionaries applied to news-conference transcripts (prosocial mean 1.60 percent, SD 0.37).
key_findings: Simple correlations with approval are negative for both agency (r = -0.16, p < 0.05) and communion (r = -0.36, p < 0.001). Hypothesis 1 not supported. Table 2, p.7.
With all controls (Model 3), agency is a significant negative predictor (beta -0.11, p < 0.05) and communion is not (beta +0.04). Table 2, p.7.
Prosocial language correlates r = +0.55 (p < 0.001) with approval and stays a positive predictor with controls (beta +0.14, p < 0.05). Table 3, p.8. Supports Hypothesis 2.

Prosocial and agency correlations differ significantly (z = 7.89, p < 0.001); communion and agency also differ (z = 2.18, p = 0.03), but both are negative. The authors read this as support for Hypothesis 3b. Results, p.8.
Media tone carries indirect effects: agency B = -0.11 [-0.30, -0.02], communion -0.06 [-0.16, -0.01], prosocial +1.82 [0.17, 5.26]. Direct effects of all three are also significant. Table 4, p.8.

Moderation (text only; numbers are in the Supplement): agency predicts disapproval only when Congress is male-dominated; communal language is approved when Congress is male-dominated and disapproved otherwise; prosocial effect is stronger with fewer men and more Republicans. Results, p.8. The authors call these results mixed.

Exploratory stepwise regression keeps 8 of 63 LIWC categories. Positive: tentativeness beta 0.46, prepositions 0.41, humans 0.25, anxiety 0.24, positive emotion 0.24, numbers 0.15. Negative: second-person pronouns -0.18, conjunctions -0.26 (p < 0.005 or better). Table 5, p.8.

Media tone mediates three of the eight: prepositions indirect B = 1.90 [0.30, 5.02], humans 2.40 [0.45, 6.03], conjunctions -3.51 [-8.77, -0.45]. Not significant for tentativeness, anxiety, positive emotion, numbers or second person. Table 6, pp.9-10.
Human words correlate with prosocial words r = 0.519 (p < 0.001). Conjunction density correlates with sentence length (r = 0.24) and negatively with six-letter word density (r = -0.38). p.11.

Headline claim: prosocial (helping) language predicts approval more strongly than agentic language, which the authors read as warmth outweighing competence even in a professional setting. Abstract; Discussion, p.9.
limitations: Correlational design: no causal inference. Reverse causation is raised (for example members bonding more when approval falls). Discussion, pp.9-10.
Third variables: only the listed controls are used. Political orientation, public age and gender are not controlled, and unidentified variables may suppress an agency effect. p.10.
Approval is dichotomous (approve or disapprove), which may miss variation. p.3.
Gallup coverage is 198 of 227 months; the rest are linearly interpolated. p.3.
Agency and communion weights come from five coders at category level; robustness is claimed only in the Supplement. p.3.
No belonging dictionary was built, so the belonging-versus-helping split is tested only with Hart et al 2011 dictionaries, in the Supplement. p.10.
The 63-category stepwise analysis is exploratory with no out-of-sample test; the authors say each result is merely suggestive until replicated. p.10.
Conjunction and sentence-complexity results are described as inconclusive. p.11.
Count inconsistency: 22 excluded plus 206 retained is 228 transcripts, but the text says 227 months. Flagged, not resolved. pp.2-3.
Only the House is analysed; no Senate data; the window ends in November 2014.
Hypothesis 3 comparisons involve two negative correlations, which the authors acknowledge complicates the reading. p.8.
short_quotes: We found that neither agentic nor communal language positively predicted public approval.
To be clear, our approach is correlational, precluding the possibility of causal inference.
The American public approved of Congress more when its members spoke about helping, but not when they spoke about belonging.

summary_md: Decter-Frain and Frimer (Frontiers in Psychology 2016) ask whether the language spoken on the House floor tracks public approval of Congress. They built a monthly series from January 1996 to November 2014 (N = 206 months, about 124 million words) and scored it with LIWC 2007. Agency and communion indexes come from five coders who weighted each category (ICC 0.82 and 0.90). A separate 127-word prosocial (helping) dictionary is scored alongside them. The outcome is monthly Gallup approval. Both broad indexes correlate negatively with approval: agency r = -0.16 and communion r = -0.36. With controls, agency stays negative (beta -0.11) and communion is null. Prosocial language correlates r = +0.55 and survives the controls (beta +0.14). Media tone partly mediates all three. An exploratory stepwise pass keeps 8 of 63 categories, and the authors call these only suggestive. Moderation by the gender and party make-up of the chamber flips some signs. The design is correlational, aggregate and chamber-level, and the authors rule out causal claims. For Paul's systems the sharpest point is about construct definition. Communion is not one thing. The helping facet and the broader communion or belonging facet behave in opposite directions against an audience-perception outcome. Melange's persona channel uses one communion share from an LLM cue codebook (empathy and compassion), and that share feeds receptivity at PERSONA_W 0.30. That codebook already sits close to the helping facet, which is reassuring. But the paper's outcome is public approval of the institution, not a member's openness to lobbying, so it neither validates nor undercuts the susceptibility mapping. It also offers a cheap dictionary-based second path for checking the LLM cue shares.

bearings.paper_claim: Broad communion correlates r = -0.36 with monthly Gallup approval (Model 3 beta +0.04, n.s.) while the prosocial helping facet correlates r = +0.55 (Model 3 beta +0.14, p < 0.05). Agency r = -0.16 and Model 3 beta -0.11 (p < 0.05). Window Jan 1996 to Nov 2014, N = 206 House months. Pooled over the whole chamber, not stratified.
bearings.system_side: The persona channel forms a z blend of two LLM cue shares from agency_communion_llm.py: persona z = 0.60 z(communion) - 0.40 z(agency). It is blended into susceptibility at PERSONA_W 0.30 for members with at least 15 classified sentences (510 of the 526 rows in agency_communion.json meet this). The communion share uses the Empathy and Compassion codebook: STRONG cues name concrete disadvantaged people, while WEAK cues include empathic focus on communities and states. Group-intimacy or belonging talk has no dedicated cue.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper is about an aggregate chamber-month audience outcome (approval of Congress), not member-level susceptibility to lobbyists. The facet lesson transfers only as a construct-definition check: a pooled communion score can mix facets with opposite signs. Ecological inference from chamber months to individual members is not licensed.

Code checked: persona formula, PERSONA_W default 0.30, 15-sentence floor, and the codebook cue tiers. Corrections: 526 is the total row count and 510 meet the threshold; the channel uses agency as well as communion; the belonging gap holds only as dedicated-cue absence, since community-focused empathy is a WEAK communion cue. The brain ruling about a failed panel of 3 or more raters was not checked.

His stated component position (from Birkenmaier and Lechner) stresses codebook-based cue design and worries about the step from trait to node. This paper supports that worry from another angle: how communion is defined, as helping versus belonging, changes the sign of its audience effect. Nothing here makes the current system stale, and the B&L communion codebook already leans toward the helping facet.

related.why: Same agency and communion constructs for politicians. Birkenmaier and Lechner use LLM cue prompting, the instrument Melange runs; this paper uses coder-weighted LIWC dictionaries. Together they give two measurement paths.

Both score Congressional Record House floor speech over 1996 to 2014 with closed-vocabulary categories. Ramey does it at member level for traits, and this paper does it at chamber-month level for approval. Verified in the Ramey item.
LIWC word-category densities as psychological indicators are the measurement basis of this paper.
Meta-analysis of how far LIWC categories carry Big Five signal. It bounds how much the coder-weighted LIWC agency and communion indexes can mean.

The PoliPers framework for politicians' agency and communion profiles is the source of the codebook Melange uses, per the agency_communion_llm.py docstring. This paper adds the belonging versus helping split.
Also treats parliamentary rhetoric as aimed at an outside audience, but works on emotive language where this paper works on agentic and communal language.
Emotional expression in congressional speech linked to legislative effectiveness at member level; this paper links language to chamber-level approval.
Politician personality and media visibility relate to this paper's finding that media tone mediates the language-approval link.
